questions.heading: An Outage Is a Binary per Substation and Year, Linked to the Units It Serves
questions.stem: A teammate wants to add $300k to every unit's replacement cost instead of adding outage variables. Why does the page reject that?

options.text: It makes the budget row nonlinear, since the cost multiplies x
options.says: The page: with $300k added to each c_i the budget row stays linear.

options.text: The outage is paid once per substation-year, however many units
options.says: Right: a shared fixed charge, which no coefficient on x can state.

options.text: It makes the model too large, with a new cost row for every unit
options.says: The page: the change adds no variable and no row.

options.text: It moves the outage into the objective, where no budget sees it
options.says: The page: the money lands in the budget row, where c_i already is.

questions.heading: An Outage Is a Binary per Substation and Year, Linked to the Units It Serves
questions.stem: Substation S has four candidates. Compare one row, the sum of their four x at most 4 times o, with four rows, each x at most o. Which 0-1 plans does each form allow?

options.text: The one row allows more, since it can leave o at 0 with units on
options.says: With o at 0 the single row forces all four x to 0.

options.text: The four rows allow more, since each unit is linked on its own
options.says: Both forms allow exactly the same 0-1 plans.

options.text: Both allow the same 0-1 plans; their LP relaxations differ
options.says: Right: same integer plans, different LP relaxations (lesson 6.7.1).

options.text: Neither allows two units at S in a year, since o is binary
options.says: With o at 1 both forms allow any of the four units.

questions.heading: Pricing the Outage Bundles the Work; the Region Limit Then Spreads It
questions.stem: Two runs, each stopped within 2% of a bound near $470,000k, report values $300k apart; one has a rule the other lacks. What may you conclude about the rule's cost?

options.text: Little, since a 2% gap is far wider than $300k
options.says: Right: the solver may stop at either value with a better plan unfound.

options.text: It costs $300k, since both runs reported OPTIMAL
options.says: OPTIMAL here means within 2%; the page calls a $283k difference noise.

options.text: It costs nothing, since the values are within 0.1%
options.says: The runs bound the cost by several $1,000k and say no more.

options.text: It costs the gap, since the solver stops exactly at 2%
options.says: The solver stops once within 2%; the ten-year plan stopped at 0.84%.
